title: Texas A&M AgriLife tests far-ultraviolet light to prevent bird flu in poultry

analysis.time: The study is set to begin in February 2026 and will span two years, with trials conducted under summer and winter conditions. The HPAI outbreak began around 2022 and is still ongoing in Texas wildlife.
analysis.location_and_population: The research is being conducted at the Texas A&M Department of Poultry Science’s Farm Complex, which includes facilities for testing far-UVC light in commercial poultry houses. The affected population includes poultry farms in the U.S., particularly in Texas, where HPAI has been reported.
analysis.event: Researchers from Texas A&M AgriLife are testing far-ultraviolet (far-UVC) light as a potential method to reduce airborne pathogens, including HPAI, in commercial poultry houses without harming the birds. This is part of a multiyear study led by Morgan Farnell, Ph.D., and Ziteng 'Tim' Xu, Ph.D.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of far-UVC light in reducing infections and economic losses in the poultry supply chain. It is expected to provide insights into how this technology could improve bird health and reduce mortality. The risk of HPAI is considered significant, as it has caused substantial losses in the poultry industry.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The research is in the testing phase, with trials planned for the next two years. The study will measure the impact of far-UVC light on pathogens like HPAI and assess its effects on bird behavior, growth, and productivity. The findings will inform potential applications of the technology in poultry facilities and possibly other animal operations.

analysis.brief_en: Researchers at Texas A&M AgriLife are testing far-ultraviolet (far-UVC) light as a potential method to reduce airborne pathogens, including highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), in commercial poultry houses without harming the birds. This study, led by Morgan Farnell, Ph.D., and Ziteng 'Tim' Xu, Ph.D., is part of a multiyear effort to develop new tools for the poultry industry. The HPAI outbreak, which began around 2022, has caused significant economic losses, prompting the need for alternative methods to control the virus. The research will examine the effectiveness of far-UVC light in real-world conditions, including its impact on bird health and productivity. The study will span two years, with trials conducted under both summer and winter conditions. If successful, the technology could be applied beyond poultry facilities to swine and dairy operations, offering a promising solution to reduce infections and improve animal welfare.

title: Rospticesoyuz explained the registration of chickens by the need to protect against avian flu

analysis.time: The measure was announced on September 3, 2026, and the registration requirement started on September 1, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Russia, private subsidiary farms with more than 10 heads of poultry, including chickens, ducks, geese, turkeys, guinea fowls, quails, and ostriches.
analysis.event: Rospticesoyuz explained the registration of chickens as a measure to protect against avian flu, with the Director General, Galina Bobyleva, stating that the registration is necessary for biosafety and safety control.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The measure applies to all poultry owners, including those with small numbers of birds, and aims to prevent the spread of avian influenza outbreaks. It is part of a broader regulatory initiative to improve biosafety and control.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The registration process is being implemented through the state veterinary service, and the government is evaluating the regulatory framework. The Rosselkhoznadzor clarified that birds do not need to be transported for registration, and the process is ongoing with proposals for improvement.

analysis.brief_en: Rospticesoyuz, a Russian poultry association, announced on September 3, 2026, that mandatory registration of poultry is necessary to protect against avian influenza. The measure, effective from September 1, 2026, applies to all poultry owners, including those with small numbers of birds, and aims to enhance biosafety and safety control. Registration can be done through the state veterinary service at the owner's place of residence, and the Rosselkhoznadzor clarified that birds do not need to be transported for registration. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev instructed relevant ministries to evaluate the regulatory framework for poultry registration, with proposals for improvement expected. This initiative is part of broader efforts to manage avian influenza outbreaks and ensure compliance with safety protocols.
analysis.summary_en: Rospticesoyuz, a Russian poultry association, announced on September 3, 2026, that mandatory registration of poultry is necessary to protect against avian influenza. The measure, effective from September 1, 2026, applies to all poultry owners, including those with small numbers of birds, and aims to enhance biosafety and safety control. Registration can be done through the state veterinary service at the owner's place of residence, and the Rosselkhoznadzor clarified that birds do not need to be transported for registration. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev instructed relevant ministries to evaluate the regulatory framework for poultry registration, with proposals for improvement expected. This initiative is part of broader efforts to manage avian influenza outbreaks and ensure compliance with safety protocols.
